title: Florida BleachWatch Program Enlists Citizen Divers to Monitor Coral Bleaching Ahead of 2026 Summer Heat Season
detail: Ahead of what scientists warn could be another extreme thermal stress season for Florida's coral reefs, WUWF (NPR public radio) reported on May 22, 2026 that the Florida Department of Environmental Protection's BleachWatch volunteer monitoring program is actively recruiting snorkelers and divers to help researchers track coral bleaching across the Florida Reef Tract — the only living barrier reef system in the continental United States. The Florida Reef Tract spans approximately 360 miles from the Dry Tortugas to Martin County and has lost more than 90% of its coral cover since the 1970s due to warming oceans, disease outbreaks, hurricanes, and pollution. Volunteer monitors are trained to distinguish normal coral coloration from early bleaching and partial bleaching, submitting geo-tagged reports that scientists integrate into the broader NOAA Coral Reef Watch data stream. The Florida Keys bleaching season typically runs from July through October, with peak thermal stress occurring in August and September. Conservation scientists note that early detection via dense citizen-science monitoring networks can accelerate rescue-and-transplant interventions, helping to preserve heat-sensitive coral genotypes before mass mortality events.

media.caption: Florida citizen scientists help track coral bleaching ahead of the 2026 summer heat season

title: Six First Nations and Canada Announce Historic 'Mia-yaltwa Ha'lidzogm hoon' Marine Protected Area on BC's Central Coast
detail: On May 22, 2026, six First Nations — Wuikinuxv, Nuxalk, Kitasoo Xai'xais, Heiltsuk, Gitxaała, and Gitga'at — signed a landmark conservation agreement with the Government of Canada and the Province of British Columbia to establish a National Marine Conservation Area Reserve (NMCAR) simultaneously designated as an Indigenous Protected and Conserved Area (IPCA) with the same geographic footprint. Named 'Mia-yaltwa Ha'lidzogm hoon' — meaning 'Realm of the Salmon, Home of the Salmon' in a composite of the six First Nations' languages — the area covers the Central Coast of British Columbia, a region of extraordinary marine biodiversity encompassing critical habitat for Pacific salmon, orca, humpback whales, Pacific herring, Dungeness crab, and diverse seabirds. This represents the first time in Canadian history that an NMCAR and an IPCA share the exact same geographic footprint, creating a dual-protection legal framework that simultaneously affirms Indigenous sovereignty and stewardship rights alongside federal conservation law. The agreement is the result of over two decades of advocacy and negotiation by the six coastal First Nations, who have been stewards of BC's central coast waters since time immemorial. Co-management structures will prioritize Indigenous governance, cultural practices, and long-term ecological health. The new protected area advances Canada's international commitments under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (30x30) and represents a model for reconciliation-based marine conservation.

media.caption: Six First Nations and Canada sign historic marine conservation area on BC's Central Coast — named 'Realm of the Salmon, Home of the Salmon'
